explain: It offers RAG-oriented evaluation components. Match each selected metric to its required contexts, answers, references, and judge inputs, then pin the implementation. Do not assume every metric is reference-free or equivalent across versions.
example: Evaluate whether an answer uses its provided context while separately testing whether retrieval found the right context.
takeaway: Name the metric's exact question before interpreting its score.

explain: It provides model-testing and metric abstractions that can integrate with Python testing workflows. Choose criteria suited to the task and retain deterministic service assertions alongside judged language checks. Record judge and dataset versions.
example: A language metric checks the response while a database assertion checks that exactly one approved record exists.
takeaway: Model evaluation complements ordinary software tests.

explain: Configuration-driven providers and assertions can make repeated prompt or model comparisons convenient. Review provider behavior, test data, external effects, and which assertions are deterministic versus judge-based.
example: Run the same synthetic missing-date cases through several configurations and compare both schema failures and invented dates.
takeaway: Experiment convenience does not replace rubric design.

explain: LangSmith, Phoenix, and TruLens support different tracing, feedback, and experiment workflows. Trace visibility helps explain failures, but platform adoption still needs reviewed instrumentation, access, and retention.
example: Link a low-support score to the retrieved passages and model version without exporting the customer's full private record.
takeaway: Visibility and evaluation are related but different responsibilities.

Q: How can two libraries disagree on the same answer?
explain: They may use different inputs, claim decomposition, rubrics, judge models, thresholds, or scales. Align those contracts before comparing numbers. A shared metric name alone does not establish comparability.
example: One metric grades answer relevance while another grades support from context. Their disagreement may be appropriate.
takeaway: Read the measurement definition, not only the label.

Q: What should a portable evaluation record contain?
explain: Store a case ID, task input, allowed evidence and expected outcomes, relevant references, dataset version, configuration identity, and result status. Preserve deterministic checks separately from judge scores. Export ordinary machine-readable records so an experiment remains inspectable outside the original platform.
example: One JSONL row records the answer, citation spans, model and prompt versions, ownership-check result, judge result, and any judge timeout. A timeout is unknown or failed evaluation, not score zero by accident.
takeaway: The evidence of an evaluation should survive a library change.

Q: When can a judge result be reused?
explain: Reuse requires compatible evaluated content, rubric, judge model and configuration, and any evidence used by the metric. Cache identity must include those dependencies and respect data retention and access scope. Changing a metric implementation can change scores even if its name stays the same. Calibrate before treating reused numbers as comparable.
example: A revised rubric now requires date applicability. Old faithfulness judgments that ignored dates cannot be reused as proof that the new rule passes.
takeaway: Evaluation caching needs the same lineage discipline as model experiments.
